planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist to wet soil in full sun to part shade; Rosy Camphorweed tolerates moderate salt exposure, suiting it to a Gulf Coast marsh-edge or ditch planting.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in moist to wet soil; Rosy Camphorweed is a Gulf Coast native found in wet savannas, pine flatwoods, and marsh or pond edges from Texas to Georgia, with moderate tolerance for brackish and saline conditions. It blooms June through July with clusters of pink-to-purple flower heads on stems 1-3 feet tall, drawing butterflies and bees strongly during its bloom period. It is a good choice for a rain garden, ditch bank, or wet pollinator bed where many other Gulf Coast natives would struggle with standing water.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Narrowleaf Yellowtop tolerates salt spray and brief brackish flooding, suiting coastal Gulf plantings.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained to moist soil; Narrowleaf Yellowtop is native to coastal central and south Florida, tolerating salt spray and brief brackish inundation at mangrove and tidal-marsh edges. It forms a mounding shrub 2-3 feet tall and 3-4 feet wide that erupts into hundreds of small yellow flower heads through fall and winter, drawing an unusually wide range of butterflies and moths during a season when fewer other natives are blooming. In the cooler end of its hardiness range it is likely root-hardy rather than fully evergreen, dying back and resprouting from the base after a hard freeze.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Chapman's Goldenrod is a clump-former, unlike the many rhizomatous goldenrods that spread aggressively.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, sandy soil; Chapman's Goldenrod is nearly endemic to the Florida peninsula and southeastern Georgia's dry sandy scrub and flatwoods, unusual among goldenrods for preferring dry rather than moist sites. It forms a well-behaved, non-rhizomatous clump reaching 3-5 feet, blooming from summer into fall with the typical bright yellow goldenrod flower clusters that draw a wide range of pollinators. Its clumping habit makes it a far better-mannered garden choice than the aggressively spreading goldenrod species, suiting a mixed native border without fear of it taking over.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist to wet soil in full sun; Southern Seaside Goldenrod specializes in tidal and maritime marsh rather than open dunes, suiting a brackish-wet Gulf Coast site.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, salt-tolerant soil; Southern Seaside Goldenrod was recently split from the already-present seaside goldenrod (Solidago sempervirens) by modern floristic treatments, and is ecologically distinct, specializing in tidal and maritime marsh habitat rather than open dunes. It forms a non-running, clump-forming plant with flowering stalks reaching 4-8 feet, blooming in fall with the classic bright yellow goldenrod display that strongly attracts late-season pollinators. It is a better fit than the dune-specialist seaside goldenrod for a brackish, consistently wet Gulf Coast marsh-edge planting.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, sandy soil in full sun; Pineland Chaffhead is narrowly endemic to central and south Florida pine flatwoods and seepage slopes, with limited commercial nursery availability.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist, sandy soil; Pineland Chaffhead grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, savannas, and seepage slopes across roughly a dozen central and south Florida counties, sending up leafless flowering stalks topped by purple flower heads from late summer into early fall. It draws a strong following of butterflies and moths during its bloom period, making it a worthwhile addition to a Florida or Gulf Coast native pollinator planting. Commercial availability is thin, generally limited to specialty Florida native-plant nurseries rather than mainstream retail, so confirm current stock before planning a planting around it.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Mock Vervain has an unusually long bloom window from late winter through midsummer.

directions: Plant in full sun in sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil; Pink Mock Vervain is native to the western Gulf coastal plain, from central, east, and south Texas into Oklahoma, Arkansas, and northeastern Mexico, favoring open prairie and woodland-edge sites. Its low, decumbent habit stays under a foot tall while spreading into a loose mat, blooming pink to lavender from February through July, an unusually long window compared to many native wildflowers. It makes a nice smaller-scale companion to the already-popular Glandularia bipinnatifida in a dry, sunny native groundcover planting, and is generally sourced through regional native-plant specialty nurseries.
